analysis.one_liner: Pays landowners when endangered species and wetlands rules cut their property's value.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a Senate committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten how two big environmental laws — the Endangered Species Act and the Clean Water Act's wetlands permit program — apply to private land. Federal agencies would have to follow state and tribal laws, get written permission before entering land to collect data, let owners dispute that data, and offer appeals of permit denials and penalties. Most significantly, any owner whose property lost $10,000 or 20% of its value because of a final federal decision could demand compensation from the agency, paid out of federal funds, with binding arbitration to settle the amount. The bill never left the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Private property owners whose land is restricted to protect endangered species or wetlands. Small landowners gain appeal rights, notice, and a say in habitat agreements, but the money flows mostly to owners of large or developable parcels: anyone losing $10,000 or 20% of a parcel's value could require the government to buy the land outright or pay the difference in value, with the amount set by binding arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of restricted land, especially large holders

how_it_helps.text: Owners losing $10,000 or 20% or more of a parcel's fair market value due to a final agency action become entitled to compensation: the agency must stay its decision and offer either to buy the land at unrestricted value or pay the difference, with binding arbitration if the owner rejects both offers.
Agencies must comply with state and tribal laws when enforcing the Endangered Species Act and wetlands permitting, and must administer them in the way that least affects property owners' rights.

Federal officials cannot enter private land to collect information without the owner's written consent, and owners get access to any data collected and a chance to dispute its accuracy before the government uses it.

Owners gain an administrative appeal — decided by a different official, held near the property — of wetlands permit decisions, penalties, and restoration orders, and of critical habitat designations, incidental take permit denials, and use restrictions under the Endangered Species Act.
Private owners and lessees must be notified and given a chance to participate in federal-state species management agreements that restrict land use.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would fund the compensation payments and land purchases required whenever endangered species or wetlands protections reduce a parcel's value past the thresholds, and the public, which bears the cost of weakened federal enforcement of species and wetland protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and the public's environmental protections

drawbacks.text: The compensation mandate shifts the cost of protecting endangered species and wetlands from the land being protected onto the federal treasury, so every significant habitat restriction becomes a government purchase or payment.

Requiring agencies to follow state and tribal laws and to choose the enforcement path that 'least affects' property rights could let state rules and owner-friendly interpretations override federal species and water protections.

Compensation amounts would be settled by arbitration before an arbitrator the agency selects from an American Arbitration Association list, and the decision binds the agency as to both whether compensation is owed and how much.

Agencies that lose a later constitutional takings case must repay the Treasury from their own appropriations for the following two fiscal years, giving agencies a budgetary reason to avoid protective decisions in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The procedural protections — consent before entry, data review, local administrative appeals, participation in management agreements — are reasonable on their face and would help small landowners caught up in federal permitting. The compensation scheme is the heart of the bill, and it is expensive by design: it converts habitat and wetland restrictions into federal payouts, and combined with the state-law compliance mandate and the agency budget penalty, it would make the underlying environmental protections much harder to enforce. The cost falls on taxpayers and on the public's interest in species and wetland protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby of Alabama introduced the bill on June 24, 1997, joined by Sens. Don Nickles and Kay Bailey Hutchison.
Four Republican senators signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats did.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the same day.
The action record shows no further activity of any kind — no hearing, no committee report, no vote — for the remaining year and a half of the 105th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species and wetland protections continued to apply unchanged, so the public and conservation interests kept the status quo. Property owners and developers who would have gained a federal compensation entitlement got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing species and wetland protections stayed intact

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — seven in all, with no Democratic support — and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landowners
industries.note: They would gain a federally funded compensation entitlement whenever species or wetland rules cut a parcel's value by $10,000 or 20%, plus the option to force a government buyout at unrestricted value. That gain comes directly at the expense of taxpayers and of the environmental protections that restricted the land.

Large working-land owners would benefit from the compensation entitlement, the administrative appeals, and the requirement that agencies defer to state law and choose the least restrictive enforcement path. Some would receive genuine relief from rules that can fall heavily on working land, but the public pays for it either through payouts or weakened protection.

The bill would make endangered species and wetland protections costlier to apply and easier to appeal, defer to state law, and dilute in enforcement — weakening the conservation outcomes these interests exist to defend.
